Techniques Used: Classification of submanifolds with planar geodesics
Schur's Bow Lemma for space curves
Study of focal radius and extrinsic diameter
Data & Platforms: Mn(κ) (Simply-connected space forms: Euclidean space Rn, unit sphere Sn, hyperbolic n-space)
FP l (Projective spaces over R, C, H, O)
Application Areas: Inverse Invariant Theory and Algebra Generation
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Algebraic-Metric Correspondence: Establishing bijections between geometric structures and algebraic ideals, specifically proving that infinitesimal manifold submetries correspond one-to-one with maximal Laplacian sub-algebras of polynomial rings to solve inverse invariant theory problems.

Symmetry-Reduced Convex Analysis: Extending Kostant’s Convexity Theorem to general submetries with 'fat sections' using Alexandrov geometry, thereby characterizing G-invariant convex subsets and enabling equivariant spectrahedral descriptions for dimension reduction in optimization.

Extrinsic Geometric Rigidity: Utilizing Schur's Bow Lemma and the classification of submanifolds with planar geodesics to prove that the minimum ratio of extrinsic diameter to focal radius (value 2) uniquely identifies totally umbilical spheres and Veronese embeddings of projective spaces.

Spectral-Volume Duality: Deriving explicit formulas for the volume of leaf spaces in singular Riemannian foliations by analyzing the pole of the Hilbert series of associated Laplacian algebras, linking asymptotic eigenvalue growth (Weyl’s law) to rational volume ratios.
Summary Description: Ricardo Mendes is a mathematician specializing in the intersection of differential geometry, invariant theory, and convex optimization. His research leverages metric geometry and spectral analysis to characterize the structure of orbit spaces and singular Riemannian foliations. Key contributions include establishing algebraic criteria for invariant algebras via Laplacian sub-algebras, extending Kostant’s Convexity Theorem to broader geometric contexts, and proving rigidity results for submanifolds in space forms. Mendes also bridges abstract geometry with computational applications by demonstrating equivariant spectrahedral descriptions for symmetric convex sets, facilitating efficient optimization. His work fundamentally connects the spectral properties of Laplacian operators on singular spaces to their geometric volumes and algebraic invariants.
